sandhi.note: The t of किञ्चित् stays t before the t of त्वया (written as a double t); then ā + u → o.
-aḥ before the voiced n becomes -o; visarga before c becomes ś; a + a → ā.

morph.note: Past participle of √वद् with samprasāraṇa (va → u) and the connecting i: उद्-इत. Synonymous with उक्तम् in the first half; the line says the same thing twice, positively and negatively.
तद् + दृश ‘looking like that’: the pronoun stem lengthens its vowel (ता-) before दृश. ‘Such’, i.e. of the same rank as Śumbha.

mantras.anvaya: त्वया सत्यम् उक्तम्; अत्र त्वया किञ्चित् मिथ्या न उदितम्। शुम्भः त्रैलोक्याधिपतिः, निशुम्भः च अपि तादृशः (अस्ति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two passive statements with the participles उक्तम् and उदितम् (verb ‘is’ understood), then two nominal sentences.
mantras.lit: Truth has been spoken by you; nothing false at all has been uttered by you here. Śumbha is the overlord of the three worlds, and Niśumbha too is such.
mantras.tr: What you say is true; you have spoken no falsehood here. Śumbha is lord of the three worlds, and Niśumbha is his equal.

comm.t: The Devī begins by granting everything the messenger has said about the brothers’ power. She does not dispute their rank; her objection will lie elsewhere.

Read with the smile of 5.116, the concession is ironic: she accepts the facts in order to bring in a condition the facts cannot meet. Note that 5.128, as the Gita Press prints it, does not repeat the phrase निशुम्भश्चापि तादृशः, though other witnesses read it there too (see 5.128).

samasa.vigraha: अल्पा बुद्धिः यस्याः सा अल्पबुद्धिः; तस्याः भावः अल्पबुद्धित्वम्, तस्मात्
samasa.literal: from the state of being one whose understanding is small

morph.note: Passive present of √कृ: the root becomes क्रि- before the passive -य- (क्रियते). With मिथ्या: ‘is made false’; with कथम्, ‘how can it be made false?’.
Passive imperative of √श्रु (the root vowel lengthened before -य-: श्रूय-): ‘let it be heard’, the polite form of ‘hear’.
Ablative of cause with the abstract -त्व: ‘because of being of small understanding’. Feigned modesty: compare अनालोचिता ‘unconsidered’ in 5.128.

mantras.anvaya: किं तु अत्र यत् प्रतिज्ञातं, तत् कथं मिथ्या क्रियते? अल्पबुद्धित्वात् (मया) पुरा या प्रतिज्ञा कृता, (सा) श्रूयताम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A rhetorical question built on a relative pair (यत् … तत्), then a passive imperative whose subject प्रतिज्ञा has a relative clause (या कृता पुरा).
mantras.lit: But here — what has been vowed, how is that to be made false? Let the vow be heard which was made formerly out of little understanding.
mantras.tr: But in this matter there is a vow I made, and how could I break it? Hear the promise I once made, foolishly.
mantras.tr_note: The passive constructions are turned active (‘I made’, ‘could I break’); the agent ‘I’ is implied by the context.

comm.t: The Devī introduces an obstacle: a vow she made long ago. She cannot make it false, and she calls it the product of her ‘little understanding’.

The self-deprecation is read as irony matching her inward smile (5.116): the Goddess who is praised as बुद्धि itself (5.20) claims to have acted from small understanding. The vow is not a mistake but the trap into which the asuras will walk.

samasa.literal: one whose strength is counter (to mine)
samasa.sense: one equal to me in strength
samasa.alt: Also read as a prādi tatpuruṣa, प्रतिगतं बलम् ‘a counter-force’, used of a person; the bahuvrīhi suits the masculine agreement.

morph.note: Present tense in a general relative clause with future sense: ‘whoever conquers (= shall conquer) me’. The main clause has the future भविष्यति.
Nominative singular of the agent noun भर्तृ (√भृ ‘to bear, support’ + -तृ): literally ‘supporter, maintainer’, the ordinary word for ‘husband’.
वि + अप + √ऊह् ‘push away, dispel’. The root is listed as ātmanepada; the parasmaipada व्यपोहति is the usual epic form.

mantras.anvaya: यः मां संग्रामे जयति, यः मे दर्पं व्यपोहति, यः लोके मे प्रतिबलः (अस्ति), सः मे भर्ता भविष्यति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three relative clauses, each opened by यः, all taken up by the single correlative सः of the main clause.
mantras.lit: He who conquers me in battle, he who removes my pride, he who is my match in strength in the world — he will be my husband.
mantras.tr: “He who conquers me in battle, who humbles my pride, who is my equal in strength in all the world — he shall be my husband.”
mantras.tr_note: Set in quotation marks as the words of the vow announced in 5.119.

comm.t: The vow itself, in three conditions that come to one: the husband must defeat her in battle, break her pride, and match her strength. The repetition of यः … यः … यः gives it the form of a formal pledge.

Since the text has already shown her to be the power of all the gods together (2.9–30) and the power present in all beings (5.14–80), no one can meet the condition. The tradition reads the vow as a statement of her sovereignty: the Goddess is not won as a possession, and her only ‘husband’ would be her equal.
A modern reading: the Devī answers a claim of ownership with a test of strength. She does not argue with Śumbha’s logic of jewels; she changes the terms on which it can be applied.

morph.note: Imperative of √ग्रह्, ninth class, with samprasāraṇa (ग्रह् → गृह्) before -णा-: गृह्णातु. पाणिं गृह्णातु ‘let him take (my) hand’ is the idiom for marriage (पाणिग्रहण).
Absolutive of √जि without a prefix: -त्वा. It sets the condition before the marriage: first conquer, then take the hand.
With the instrumental, किम् asks ‘what (is gained) by …?’: किं चिरेण ‘why delay?’.

mantras.anvaya: तत् शुम्भः महासुरः निशुम्भः वा अत्र आगच्छतु। मां जित्वा मे पाणिम् अत्र लघु गृह्णातु। चिरेण किम्?
mantras.anvaya_en: Two third-person imperatives (आगच्छतु, गृह्णातु), the second preceded by the absolutive जित्वा; the rhetorical किं चिरेण stands between them.
mantras.lit: So let Śumbha come here, or Niśumbha the great asura; having conquered me — what (use) is delay? — let him take my hand here quickly.
mantras.tr: So let Śumbha come here, or Niśumbha, the mighty asura. Let him conquer me and, without delay, take my hand.

comm.t: The Devī applies the vow to the proposal. Either brother may come, as Śumbha offered (5.113), but first he must defeat her; then let him marry her at once.

The urgency (किं चिरेण, लघु) mirrors the messenger’s demand that she come quickly (5.103, लघु). The invitation is a challenge: the next chapters bring first the asura generals and finally the two brothers to fight her.
